cards.front: In an otherwise well child over 6 months with uncomplicated bilateral acute otitis media, initial RCH management is analgesia plus [___].
cards.context:
Australian RCH guidance recommends analgesia and observation for most uncomplicated AOM.

Bilateral disease in a child under 2 can lower the threshold for treatment in some international guidelines, but it does not automatically mandate antibiotics under RCH guidance.

Base the decision on age, severity, systemic illness, persistence, otorrhoea or complications, high-risk features and the local antimicrobial guideline.

cards.front: A normal thymus permits visualisation of pulmonary [___] through it and never compresses the airway — unlike a mediastinal mass.
cards.context:
Two features separate a normal thymus from a mediastinal mass, and both are about what it does NOT do.

Pulmonary vessels remain visible through it because it is not very radio-opaque, and it never compresses the airway or adjacent vasculature. A mass does both.

cards.front: A child has hypoxia after blunt chest trauma despite no rib fracture. The most common intrathoracic injury is pulmonary [___].
cards.context: A child's compliant chest wall transmits blunt force to the lung parenchyma. Pulmonary contusion may cause hypoxia despite little bruising, no rib fracture and a normal early film.

cards.front: Wide [___] split S2 = atrial septal defect (ASD). Anything increasing right-sided blood flow widens the S2 split.
cards.context:
The S2 split varies normally with respiration (P2 delays during inspiration as RV stroke volume rises).

This is highly specific for ASD and is the most reliable bedside finding for the diagnosis.

cards.front: Perthes disease: idiopathic [___] of femoral head in boys aged 4-10; younger age at onset = better prognosis.
cards.context:
Perthes (Legg-Calve-Perthes) is idiopathic AVN of the femoral head in boys aged 4-10y. Blood supply interruption causes head fragmentation and collapse, then revascularisation and remodelling.

Presents with progressive hip pain, limp and a positive Trendelenburg sign. Younger onset = better prognosis because there is more remodelling time.

Long-term outcome depends on residual femoral-head deformity and joint congruence; only a minority require total hip arthroplasty by midlife.

cards.front: In utero exposure to maternal [___] during pregnancy increases a child's risk of developing asthma.
cards.context:
Asthma risk is partly programmed before birth. In utero exposure to tobacco smoke alters airway development and raises wheeze/asthma risk independent of postnatal exposure.

Family atopy and personal eczema remain the strongest predictors.

cards.front: A child's forearm film shows one cortex disrupted while the opposite side bows without breaking. This is a [___] fracture.
cards.context:
A greenstick fracture reflects the pliability of paediatric bone: tension breaks one cortex while the opposite cortex bends.

A buckle fracture instead compresses and wrinkles the cortex without a complete cortical break.

cards.front: In the MTA trial for core ADHD symptoms (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity), the single key active treatment ingredient was medication; adding [___] therapy gave extra benefit only for non-core symptoms (anxiety, aggression).
cards.context:
The MTA trial (Multimodal Treatment of ADHD, NIMH) randomised children to medication, behaviour therapy, combined, or community care.

Combined therapy was best for non-core symptoms (anxiety, aggression, social skills, parent-child relationships).

cards.front: A child with low platelets (ITP) bleeds at the surface — bruises, petechiae, nosebleeds. A child with haemophilia instead bleeds deep, into muscles and [___].
cards.context:
Where a child bleeds is the first clue to which part of haemostasis is broken. Platelets plug small surface vessels, so too few of them (ITP) shows as surface bleeding: petechiae, bruises, nosebleeds, gum oozing.

Clotting factors stabilise bleeds in big, high-pressure spaces, so a factor problem (haemophilia) shows as deep bleeding — a swollen, painful knee or ankle after minor knocks, or a muscle bleed.

Surface = think platelets; deep = think factors.

cards.front: When plotting a preterm infant on a growth chart, subtract weeks of prematurity to obtain [___] age until 2 years.
cards.context:
A preterm infant's size reflects weeks since birth minus weeks born early — otherwise a 32-weeker plotted at 4 months chronological looks falsely small.

Corrected age = chronological age minus prematurity; use it on growth charts until age 2.

cards.front: The common self-limited newborn rash with erythematous macules and tiny pustules whose smear shows [___] is erythema toxicum neonatorum.
cards.context:
Most term newborns develop a fleeting blotchy erythematous eruption with small papules or pustules in the first days of life. It is self-limited.

When a pustule is sampled, the cells are eosinophils — a useful discriminator from infectious pustulosis (neutrophils) when you are unsure.

cards.front: Beyond hearing loss, serious neurological sequelae of bacterial meningitis include epilepsy, intellectual impairment, and [___] from obstructed CSF flow.
cards.context: Hydrocephalus follows obstruction of CSF flow/reabsorption by inflammatory exudate; it presents with a bulging fontanelle, rising head circumference, or signs of raised intracranial pressure after the acute illness.

cards.front: Where parents refuse treatment necessary to prevent serious harm, authority to treat comes from the [___], acting in the child's best interests.
cards.context:
The court's welfare jurisdiction (parens patriae) can authorise treatment over a parent's objection — classically transfusion in a Jehovah's Witness family, or a refused cancer treatment with good survival odds.

In a true emergency you treat first under the emergency doctrine and seek authority afterwards. Do not let a child deteriorate while waiting for a court.

cards.front: Unlike in some older children with bacterial meningitis, adjunctive [___] is not advised in neonates.
cards.context:
Adjunctive dexamethasone may be considered in older children with bacterial meningitis, ideally before or with the first antibiotic dose.

RCH does not advise dexamethasone in neonates because benefit is uncertain and neurodevelopmental harm is a concern.

cards.front: Amblyopia = reduced vision from abnormal visual development; critical treatment period is before age [___]; treat with patching of the better eye.
cards.context:
Amblyopia (reduced vision in one eye despite structurally normal eye) develops when one eye's input is suppressed during the critical period of visual development.

Critical period for treatment is before age 7-8 — after this, visual pathways become much less plastic and improvement is limited.

Treat with patching of the better eye.

cards.front: Beyond leukaemia and CNS tumours, the childhood-characteristic cancers are the embryonal tumours (neuroblastoma, Wilms', retinoblastoma, hepatoblastoma); adult cancer is dominated by [___].
cards.context:
Childhood cancer is dominated by leukaemia (~30%), CNS tumours (~20%), and solid tumours arising from persistent fetal tissue — neuroblastoma, nephroblastoma, retinoblastoma, hepatoblastoma.

Epithelial cancers of breast, bowel, lung, and prostate need decades of acquired mutations, so they dominate adult practice and are vanishingly rare in children.

cards.front: A stool reducing-substances test is positive when the sugar carries a free [___] or ketone group that reduces copper in the Clinitest reagent.
cards.context:
A reducing sugar carries a free aldehyde or ketone group, which donates electrons and reduces copper(II) to copper(I) — the colour change the bedside Clinitest tablet reports.

The test detects a chemically free end, not sugar in general. Glucose, galactose, fructose, lactose and maltose all qualify.

Sucrose is the exception: its reactive carbons are locked in the glycosidic bond. Sucrose malabsorption therefore tests negative, so a normal result does not exclude carbohydrate malabsorption.

cards.front: A physeal fracture that extends into the metaphysis but spares the epiphysis is Salter-Harris type [___].
cards.context: Salter-Harris II is the commonest physeal injury. Its fracture line crosses the physis and exits through the metaphysis, while the epiphysis and articular surface remain intact.

cards.front: A short teenager with delayed puberty, a delayed bone age, but a normal predicted adult height most likely has [___] delay of growth and puberty.
cards.context:
The 'late bloomer'. Bone age is delayed (lags chronological age), so there's still growth potential and the predicted adult height is normal — reassurance, not treatment.

Contrast familial short stature, where bone age matches chronological age.

cards.front: The commonest pathogen in paediatric haematogenous osteomyelitis is [___].
cards.context: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of haematogenous osteomyelitis in children. Blood cultures should be collected before antibiotics when doing so will not delay treatment.

cards.front: The resuscitation fluid bolus for a shocked child is 10–20 mL/kg of isotonic [___] (e.g. 0.9% saline).
cards.context: Separate resuscitation from maintenance. A shocked child gets a rapid bolus of isotonic crystalloid (10–20 mL/kg), reassessed after each — distinct from the slower Holliday-Segar maintenance calculation.

cards.front: PSGN: self-limiting; ~1-2 weeks after GAS pharyngitis but 3-6 weeks after impetigo; triad of hypertension, haematuria, and [___]; low C3 (normalises in 6-8 weeks).
cards.context:
PSGN follows GAS infection after a site-dependent latent period — ~1-2 weeks after pharyngitis, but 3-6 weeks after skin infection (impetigo) — from immune-complex deposition in the glomeruli.

C3 low (alternative pathway activation) but normalises within 6-8 weeks; persistent low C3 suggests another diagnosis.

cards.front: Kawasaki disease is treated with IVIG and aspirin to prevent coronary artery [___].
cards.context: The reason Kawasaki must not be missed: untreated, it damages the coronary arteries. Prompt IVIG (plus aspirin) within 10 days dramatically reduces that risk.

cards.front: The infant haemoglobin trough occurs at about 6-9 weeks of age, because the rise in arterial oxygen after birth switches off [___] production.
cards.context:
Timing is the examinable half. In a term baby the trough sits in the second and third months of life, not in the newborn period, and preterm babies reach it earlier and lower.

The mechanism explains the timing: arterial oxygen rises sharply at birth, erythropoietin production switches off, and marrow output only restarts once the haemoglobin has drifted low enough to stimulate it again.

Because it is physiological, it needs no iron and no investigation in a thriving baby.

cards.front: ADING separates [___], which is what the child takes in, from growth, which is the plotted trajectory that results.
cards.context:
Nutrition and growth are deliberately separate letters, because they answer different questions. Nutrition is what goes in — breast or formula, volumes, solids, appetite, food refusal.

 Growth is the plotted result over time.

A growth chart cannot tell you about intake, and a feeding history cannot tell you whether the child is thriving, so a history that collapses the two loses the link between them.

cards.front: A cyanosed infant whose film shows a normal-sized heart with an elevated apex, a concave pulmonary bay and decreased pulmonary vascularity has a [___]-shaped heart.
cards.context:
Tetralogy of Fallot is the cyanotic-infant film, and the shape is the diagnosis.

Right ventricular hypertrophy lifts the apex and the small pulmonary trunk leaves a concave pulmonary bay, together giving the classic outline. Heart size is usually normal, which surprises people.

cards.front: Nephrotic syndrome triad: proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and [___]; often hypercholesterolaemia from compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis.
cards.context:
Nephrotic syndrome triad: heavy proteinuria (urine protein:creatinine ratio >200 mg/mmol), hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L), oedema. Often plus hypercholesterolaemia (compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis).

Mechanism: damage to glomerular podocytes → loss of negative-charge barrier → albumin and other anionic proteins leak into urine. The oedema follows colloid pressure loss.

cards.front: To achieve a neutral airway in an infant, place a folded towel under the shoulders — the large [___] otherwise flexes the neck and obstructs the airway.
cards.context:
An infant's occiput is proportionally huge: lying flat, it flexes the neck and closes the airway you are trying to open.

A folded towel under the SHOULDERS — not the head — restores the neutral position. In an older child the target is the sniffing position instead.

Suction only what you can see, with a light: blind suction provokes laryngospasm and bradycardia.

cards.front: Infant respiratory vulnerability: smaller airways (resistance ∝ 1/radius⁴), compliant [___] walls, fewer alveoli, fetal Hb until 6 months.
cards.context:
Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius — halve the diameter, sixteen-fold the resistance. So even small amounts of mucosal oedema in an infant airway dramatically increase work of breathing.

Compliant chest walls don't generate negative pressure efficiently, fewer alveoli mean less reserve, and fetal Hb's high O2 affinity slows release at the tissue level.

cards.front: Cyanotic newborn not improving with oxygen (suspected duct-dependent CHD): start prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion to maintain ductal [___] while awaiting echo.
cards.context:
Duct-dependent CHD relies on a patent ductus arteriosus for either pulmonary flow (pulmonary/tricuspid atresia, severe pulmonary stenosis) or systemic flow (HLHS, critical aortic stenosis, coarctation).

The duct normally closes in the first days of life — exactly when these babies crash. Empirical PGE1 (alprostadil 0.01-0.05 µg/kg/min IV) keeps it open by relaxing ductal smooth muscle.

Give it to any cyanotic or collapsed neonate with duct-dependent CHD on the differential, even before echo. An unnecessary start is low-cost (apnoea, fever, hypotension); NOT starting risks a dead infant.

cards.front: Adolescents may make adult-like risk decisions when consequences are clear; differences are more likely when the situation is socially or emotionally [___].
cards.context:
The dual-systems account is a model, not a literal brain timer. Clear consequences can support adult-like choices; social, emotional, novel or ambiguous settings may expose differences.

Brain structure and function change into adulthood. Those trajectories do not establish a single birthday when judgement becomes mature.

Avoid claiming the prefrontal cortex is unfinished until 25. Assess the individual young person, the decision and its setting, rather than inferring capacity from age alone.

cards.front: The “oligo-” in oligoarticular JIA means no more than [___] joints are affected during the first six months.
cards.context: The subtype name is a counting rule: oligoarticular JIA affects a small number of joints during its first six months. More joints makes it polyarticular disease.

cards.front: In paediatric DKA, insulin infusion is started after the first [___] of fluid resuscitation to reduce cerebral oedema risk.
cards.context:
Cerebral oedema is the dominant cause of death in paediatric DKA.

Delaying insulin until after the first hour of fluid resuscitation lets perfusion restore and glucose fall gently before the rapid osmolar shift insulin causes.

Bolus insulin and rapid bicarbonate are both contraindicated.

cards.front: Empiric antibiotic choice starts with the infection [___] and likely organisms, then adjusts for patient and local-resistance factors.
cards.context:
Start with the infection site and likely organisms. Then account for age, acquisition, severity, immune status, previous cultures or colonisation, allergy, organ function and local resistance.

Coverage in vitro is not enough: the drug must reach the infected compartment and be safe for the child.

cards.front: Mid-parental height = (father + mother ± [___]) / 2 cm (add for boys, subtract for girls); target range around the predicted height is ± 8.5 cm.
cards.context:
Mid-parental height predicts adult-height genetic potential — (father + mother ± 13)/2 cm (+13 boys, −13 girls), target ±8.5 cm. The ±13 correction goes INSIDE the average (shifts parental mean 6.5 cm), not onto it.

Use to interpret growth chart positioning — 5th-percentile child with mid-parental target on 3rd is genetically small (no pathology); same child with parents on 50th is likely growth failure.

Combine with bone age (left wrist X-ray): delayed + short = constitutional delay; normal age + short with short parents = familial; delayed + short with normal parents = work up GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, coeliac.

cards.front: First-line controller for persistent paediatric asthma is [___]; before escalating dose, always review inhaler technique, adherence, and triggers.
cards.context:
ICS are first-line controller therapy for persistent paediatric asthma (reliever >2 days/wk, nocturnal symptoms >2 nights/month, FEV1 <80%, or any oral-steroid episode in the past year).

Low-dose ICS (fluticasone 50-100 µg BD, budesonide 100-200 µg BD) first-line; step up to medium-dose ICS or add LABA if uncontrolled.

Most 'uncontrolled asthma' is technique or adherence, not drug failure.

cards.front: A febrile child's film shows right-sided consolidation that obliterates the right heart border while the right hemidiaphragm stays sharp. The lobe involved is the right [___] lobe, because the preserved diaphragmatic outline excludes the lower lobe.
cards.context:
This is the silhouette sign used forwards rather than recognised backwards, which is what a viva asks for. A border is visible only because aerated lung abuts it.

 The right heart border sits against the right middle lobe, so losing that border localises the consolidation to the middle lobe.

The right hemidiaphragm sits against the lower lobe — a preserved diaphragm with a lost heart border therefore excludes lower-lobe disease, without needing a lateral film.

cards.front: Infantile haemangioma: most common benign soft tissue tumour; 3 phases — proliferative (3-6 months), plateau, involution ([___]% by age 5); first-line treatment is oral propranolol.
cards.context:
Infantile haemangiomas are the commonest benign soft tissue tumour of childhood — not usually present at birth, appear in first weeks.

Most need no treatment.

Treat (oral propranolol first-line) for: ulceration, periorbital (amblyopia risk), nasal tip (anatomic distortion), large, multiple, or symptomatic.

cards.front: Consolidation that obliterates the outline of the hemidiaphragm lies in the [___] lobe.
cards.context:
The lower lobes sit against the diaphragm, so they take the diaphragm with them.

Right lower lobe consolidation loses the outline of the right hemidiaphragm. Its basal segment lies behind the liver, where consolidation or hyperinflation may still be seen through the liver shadow.

cards.front: Greasy, yellow, adherent scale on the scalp of an otherwise well infant is [___] cap (infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis).
cards.context: Cradle cap is infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis — non-itchy and self-limiting. Soften the scale with emollient then brush gently; ketoconazole shampoo or mild hydrocortisone if persistent.

cards.front: Effortless regurgitation in a thriving, content infant that resolves by around 1 year is physiological [___].
cards.context:
The 'happy spitter': effortless posseting in a thriving, content infant from an immature lower oesophageal sphincter.

It needs reassurance, not investigation — it becomes GORD only when there's poor weight gain, distress, or complications.

cards.front: Beyond renal disease, a serious GI complication of HSP is [___] — a small-bowel telescoping causing severe colicky abdominal pain.
cards.context:
HSP intussusception is typically ileo-ileal (small-bowel), unlike the classic ileocolic intussusception of infancy, so it can be missed on the usual ultrasound windows.

Suspect it when a child with HSP develops severe colicky abdominal pain.

cards.front: The four components of tetralogy of Fallot are pulmonic [___], an overriding aorta, a ventricular septal defect and right ventricular hypertrophy.
cards.context:
The four components are the definition, and the outflow obstruction is what drives the radiology.

Pulmonic stenosis obstructs right ventricular outflow, so pulmonary vascularity falls and the right ventricle hypertrophies. The overriding aorta and ventricular septal defect complete the tetrad.

cards.front: A child's spine X-ray shows a hemivertebra at the apex of the curve. By its cause, this curve is classed as [___].
cards.context:
A vertebra that fails to form or to separate on one side in early fetal life makes the two sides of the spine grow unequally. An unsegmented bar is the other classic lesion.

A one-sided bar opposite a hemivertebra progresses fastest, while balanced anomalies, such as hemivertebrae on opposite sides, may barely progress.

Heart and kidney anomalies often travel with it, so the doctor making the diagnosis screens both systems, including a renal ultrasound.

cards.front: After casting a forearm fracture, advise parents to [___] the limb and return urgently if the fingers become numb, pale, or the cast feels tight.
cards.context: Elevation reduces oedema; if the cast becomes too tight it raises pressure in the closed forearm compartment. Parents are the monitoring system once the child goes home, so the advice is concrete and red-flag based.

cards.front: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble [___]; uses blue light (450-460 nm); avoid as treatment if primarily conjugated bilirubin is elevated.
cards.context:
Blue light at 450-460 nm converts unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble photoisomers, especially lumirubin, which bypass hepatic conjugation.

Adverse effects: temperature instability, dehydration/loose stools, retinal injury without eye protection, and bronze baby syndrome if conjugated bilirubin is high.

cards.front: A baby with tetralogy of Fallot is already cyanotic at birth. This timing points to [___] right-ventricular outflow obstruction.
cards.context:
The timing of cyanosis tracks the severity of right-ventricular outflow obstruction.

Severe obstruction produces a large right-to-left shunt immediately; milder obstruction can leave a pink newborn who becomes cyanotic later.

cards.front: A large pleural effusion displaces the mediastinum away from the effusion, but associated pulmonary [___] may cancel the shift.
cards.context:
Mediastinal shift is the sign that tells you how much fluid there is — unless collapse cancels it out.

A large effusion pushes the trachea and mediastinum to the opposite side. Where there is associated pulmonary collapse pulling the other way, there may be no shift at all.

cards.front: In abusive head trauma the subdural haemorrhage arises when acceleration–deceleration shearing tears the [___] as they cross from the cortex to the dural venous sinuses.
cards.context:
Explains WHY the bleed is subdural rather than epidural: shaking stretches and ruptures the veins spanning the subdural space.

An infant's proportionally large head, weak neck muscles, and higher brain water content make these veins especially vulnerable — the mechanism, not just the pattern, is the point.

cards.front: [___] accounts for 80% of childhood nephrotic syndrome and is steroid-responsive.
cards.context:
Minimal change disease is the dominant cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome — ~80% in pre-pubertal children, declining with age.

Because of the strong age-based predictive value, biopsy is not done up front in a typical 1-10 y old with steroid-responsive nephrotic syndrome — empirical prednisolone for 4-6 weeks.

cards.front: A 4-year-old on penicillin for presumed scarlet fever is still febrile on day 6, now with bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection and oedema of the hands and feet. The diagnosis to exclude urgently is [___].
cards.context:
A positive GAS swab does not settle it — asymptomatic streptococcal carriage is common, and true scarlet fever defervesces quickly on penicillin.

The hinge is the criteria set: fever persisting past day 5 with non-purulent conjunctivitis and extremity oedema are features scarlet fever does not produce.

Missing the switch costs the early-IVIG window, and with it the chance to prevent coronary artery aneurysms.

cards.front: Most congenital diaphragmatic hernias are left-sided and herniate posterolaterally through the foramen of [___].
cards.context:
Side and site are both examinable, and they are not independent — the common defect is posterolateral and on the left.

Roughly 70 to 90 per cent are left-sided. A right-sided hernia is much harder to see because the liver plugs the defect and bowel is not a prominent feature, so presentation is often delayed.

cards.front: Fetal pulmonary vascular resistance is [___] (lungs are fluid-filled, not gas-exchanging). The pulmonary artery → aorta shunt is the ductus arteriosus; the right atrium → left atrium shunt is the foramen ovale.
cards.context:
Fetal lungs are fluid-filled, so pulmonary vascular resistance is HIGH — higher than systemic, because the placenta is a huge low-resistance bed. Blood shunts right-to-left, away from the lungs.

Two lung bypasses: the foramen ovale, right atrium to left, taking the best-oxygenated blood to brain and coronaries; and the ductus arteriosus, pulmonary artery to aorta.

At birth the lungs inflate, resistance falls and the placenta goes, so both shut. Trap: a duct-dependent baby looks well at birth and collapses over days as the duct closes.

cards.front: The bacterial cause of tonsillitis predicted by the Centor criteria is group A [___].
cards.context: Most sore throats in young children are viral. The bacterial cause worth treating is group A strep, which the Centor criteria (fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough) help predict before antibiotics.

cards.front: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited disorder in which the protein is [___], so it is both stuck in the liver and scarce in the blood.
cards.context:
A single inherited condition, carried on the SERPINA1 gene. The severe form is usually the PiZZ genotype, in which the protein is misfolded.

Calling it 'a deficiency' is only half the story and is the reason the liver disease surprises people: there is too little of it in the blood, AND the faulty copies get stuck in the liver cells that made them.

cards.front: Under RCH guidance, a preterm infant’s growth is plotted using corrected age until [___] years.
cards.context: Adjusting for prematurity prevents misreading a preterm infant as small for their stage of maturation. RCH uses this correction through the second birthday.

cards.front: Under the RCH pathway, late-onset neonatal sepsis without meningitis starts with IV [___] plus gentamicin, modified for MRSA or ESBL risk.
cards.context:
Late-onset infection reflects community, skin, device or hospital flora rather than only maternal flora. The RCH default without meningitis is cefazolin plus gentamicin.

This is a local empiric choice: substitute vancomycin for cefazolin when MRSA risk is present and account for known maternal or infant ESBL colonisation.

cards.front: A child with kissing tonsils has recurrent witnessed apnoeas but uncertain severity. Before choosing a treatment pathway, the objective test is a paediatric [___].
cards.context:
Kissing tonsils and witnessed apnoeas suggest obstructive sleep-disordered breathing, but tonsil size alone does not establish severity. Snoring without apnoea is a different decision.

When the clinical severity remains uncertain before selecting a treatment pathway, the Australian Sleep Association guideline supports objective testing to confirm and grade obstruction.

cards.front: Bowel that telescopes into the next segment in a 6–24 month old — intermittent colic, vomiting, late redcurrant-jelly stool — is [___].
cards.context: Bowel telescopes into the adjacent segment, peaking 6 months–2 years. The classic triad: paroxysms of colicky pain (the infant draws up the legs), vomiting, and late 'redcurrant jelly' stool (blood + mucus).

cards.front: With an intact eardrum and normal canal volume, both glue ear and acute otitis media can produce a [___] tympanogram; signs of acute inflammation separate them.
cards.context:
With an intact eardrum and normal canal volume, a flat trace supports effusion but cannot distinguish glue ear from acute otitis media.

Acute onset and inflammatory otoscopic findings support acute otitis media; glue ear lacks acute inflammation.

cards.front: A sandpaper-textured rash with a strawberry tongue following a group A strep throat is [___] fever.
cards.context: Scarlet fever follows a group A strep throat: a fine, rough 'sandpaper' rash, flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor, and a strawberry tongue. It responds to penicillin.

cards.front: The commonest cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia is [___]-hydroxylase deficiency.
cards.context: One enzyme block explains ~95% of cases: cortisol/aldosterone can't be made, so precursors shunt to androgens (virilising a female infant) and salt-wasting can cause neonatal adrenal crisis.
